question: Why does pasta take longer to cook in boiling water high up in the mountains?
source_excerpt: At higher elevations, water boils at a lower temperature because of the lower atmospheric pressure, so food takes longer to cook.

extra.why_interesting: People assume boiling water is always equally hot. In the mountains it's bubbling away and still cooler than at sea level, which explains why the pasta stays hard.
extra.verification_notes: Boiling point falls with lower air pressure at altitude, so the water is cooler and pasta cooks more slowly; this is established physics (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High-altitude_cooking).

explanation: Thinner air presses less on the water, so it boils sooner and cooler. At the top of Everest it bubbles at only about 70°C, which isn't hot enough to cook pasta properly.

question: Fresh pineapple stops a jelly dessert from setting, but tinned pineapple works perfectly. What has the tinned fruit been through that makes the difference?
source_excerpt: The heat used in the canning process destroys the enzyme, so the gelatin sets normally.

extra.why_interesting: It sounds like a strange kitchen rule, but the player can reason it out: tinned fruit differs from fresh mainly because it has been heated. The explanation then reveals the enzyme behind it.
extra.verification_notes: Canning heat denatures the protease bromelain, so tinned pineapple doesn't digest gelatin; the sources agree (https://www.science-sparks.com/jelly-will-it-set/).

explanation: Fresh pineapple contains an enzyme called bromelain that chops up the gelatin proteins holding jelly together. The heat of canning destroys it, and fresh kiwi and papaya ruin jelly in the same way.

question: A popcorn kernel explodes because of something ordinary trapped inside its hard shell. What is it?
source_excerpt: Popcorn pops because of trapped water and the pressure that builds as it turns to steam. Each kernel holds a small amount of water.

extra.why_interesting: Everyone has made popcorn, but few have asked what actually makes it explode. The player can reason it out ('what's in a seed that expands when hot?'), and the answer turns a common snack into a tiny pressure cooker.
extra.verification_notes: Popcorn pops because water inside the kernel turns to steam and bursts the hull, per https://www.sciencebuddies.org/stem-activities/explore-the-pop-in-popcorn

explanation: The drop of water inside turns to steam, and the pressure builds until the shell bursts. That's why old, dried-out kernels just sit in the pan and don't pop.

question: True or false: bread kept in the fridge goes stale faster than bread left out on the kitchen counter.
source_excerpt: Retrogradation happens at all temperatures but peaks at fridge-range temperatures, roughly 0–5°C

extra.why_interesting: Most people assume the fridge keeps food fresh longer, so they put bread in it. The surprising truth is that the cold speeds up staling, and the player learns that stale bread isn't really 'dried out' at all.
extra.verification_notes: Starch retrogradation peaks at fridge temperatures (~0–5°C), so ordinary bread stales faster refrigerated than at room temperature; no newer developments contradict this (https://wearegoodinbread.com/why-good-bread-doesnt-belong-in-the-fridge/).

explanation: Staling isn't really drying out. The starch slowly recrystallises, and fridge temperatures speed that up. The freezer stops it, which is why toast from frozen bread tastes fresh.
